title: Gate Control Improves Routing Efficiency for Periodic Traffic
authors: Hyunwook Song, Hoyun Choi, B. Kahng
abstract: Traffic movement on highways and data packet transmission across the Internet serve as prototypical examples of collective dynamical behavior in complex systems. Although enhancing traffic flow in complex networks has been extensively investigated, most existing studies focus on single-queue models. In this paper, we introduce a simple yet effective two-queue scheme with gate control that regulates vehicle entry and integrates it with the routing protocol. When vehicles arrive at a on-ramp gate, they first join a waiting queue and are permitted to enter the main flowing queue once it has emptied. This two-queue strategy is especially advantageous when highway inflow varies periodically with large fluctuations, as is commonly observed in real traffic. Moreover, it modifies the system's failure characteristics, replacing sudden, discontinuous jamming transitions with gradual, continuous ones. The approach is based on a simple rule using only local queue information, making it easy to implement and widely applicable. Beyond the specific setup studied here, it can be applied to other transportation networks under different conditions or extended to other queuing systems, such as Internet data packet routing.
summary: This paper models traffic flow on complex networks using a two-queue system and compares two control protocols: Free Entry (FE) and Restricted Entry (RE). It demonstrates that the RE protocol acts as a superior self-regulating buffer, mitigating the severity of congestion and changing the jamming transition from abrupt to gradual, especially when external demand fluctuates periodically.
main_problem: The paper investigates how regulating entry into a main flow queue, using a two-queue gate control mechanism, improves routing efficiency in complex networks subjected to periodic traffic fluctuations.
main_result: The restricted entry (RE) protocol significantly outperforms the free-entry (FE) protocol, particularly under large periodic fluctuations, by replacing sudden jamming transitions with gradual, continuous ones.
method: The analysis uses macroscopic and microscopic modeling of traffic flow, comparing the dynamics of FE and RE protocols using order parameters and time-averaged system occupancy.
model_or_system: The model simulates traffic movement on complex networks (like ER or BA graphs) using a two-queue system (waiting and flowing queues) at each node, driven by a time-varying external demand.
key_observables: Total system vehicles A(t), order parameter $\rho$ (congestion rate), and the critical transition point $p_c$.
important_parameters: Periodic fluctuation amplitude $\eta$, driving period $T$, and the traffic-awareness parameter $h$.
main_assumptions: The approach relies on a simple local rule using only local queue information, making it highly implementable.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the temporal evolution of system occupancy $A(t)$ for both protocols under varying $\eta$, and phase diagrams showing the transition point $p_c$ dependence on $\eta$ for both FE and RE.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from defining the two-queue model and protocols (FE vs. RE) to performing macroscopic analysis of congestion transitions ($\rho$ vs. $p_0$), and finally analyzing the impact of periodic forcing ($\eta > 0$) on the stability and transition characteristics.
why_interesting: The study of non-equilibrium dynamics, phase transitions (jamming), and the effect of external periodic forcing on collective behavior is directly relevant to non-equilibrium statistical mechanics and open quantum systems.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Two gate control protocols. (a) In the free-entry (FE) protocol, the gate remains open regardless of the flow- ing queue state, enabling unrestricted entry from the waiting queue. (b) In contrast, the restricted-entry (RE) protocol per- mits entry to the flowing queue only when it is empty (fi = 0).

FIG. 2. Temporal evolution of the total number of vehicles in queues, A(t), as a function of time step t with a driving period of T = 1440. Results for the free-entry (FE) protocol are shown in left column and for the restricted-entry (RE) protocol in right column. Each color represents a different amplitude η (see legend in (b)). Insets show the time average of A(t) with window length T. At intermediate p0 ((c), (d)), FE and RE exhibit opposite trends with increasing η due to the asymmetric behavior in Fig. 3(e) and (f).

FIG. 3. Order parameter ρ vs. p0, η, and T. Green dashed curves represent the transition curves pc(η) for each T. For the FE, the order parameter increases drastically beyond pc as p0 increases. This indicates that the transition is discontinuous. On the other hand, for the RE, the order parameter increases gradually beyond pc as p0 increases, indicating a continuous transition. The green cross represents the point where pc of FE and RE are same.

FIG. 4. The order parameter distribution P(ρ) at T = 1440 for the free-entry (FE, left column) and restricted-entry (RE, right column) protocols at different amplitude values η. The FE protocol displays two distinct peaks, whereas the RE pro- tocol exhibits a single peak.
